en: To make something impure or weaker by adding a cheaper or harmful substance
hook: ADULTERATE: an ADULT trick to cheat by mixing in cheap stuff.
story: The milkman's customers kept complaining that the milk looked thin. One morning, a neighbor caught him pouring tap water into the cans before delivery. He had been adulterating the milk for months to earn more money. To adulterate is to spoil the purity of something by mixing in an inferior substance, like formalin in fish or water in milk.

en: A person who publicly supports a cause; to publicly recommend or support
hook: ADVOCATE: in Bangladesh, a lawyer is literally called an 'advocate', someone who speaks FOR you.
story: Nadia became an advocate for road safety after her cousin was hit by a bus. She gave speeches at schools, wrote to newspapers, and advocated for proper zebra crossings near every college. An advocate is someone who speaks up for a person or a cause. As a verb, to advocate means to publicly argue in favor of something.

en: To increase the power, wealth, or importance of; to make something seem greater than it is
bn: ক্ষমতা বা মর্যাদা বাড়ানো; বাড়িয়ে দেখানো
hook: AG-GRAND-ize: to make yourself GRAND.
story: The local politician built a giant statue of himself at the town entrance and named three roads after his own family. Everything he did was to aggrandize himself, to make himself look bigger, richer, and more powerful. To aggrandize is to enlarge someone's power or importance, often selfishly. Self-aggrandizing people constantly exaggerate their own achievements.

en: Cheerful and eager readiness; prompt willingness
bn: উৎসাহপূর্ণ তৎপরতা; সাগ্রহে ও দ্রুত সাড়া
hook: ALACRITY: 'ALL A CRITTER' jumps up at once when food appears.
story: When the teacher asked who wanted to leave class early to help decorate for the cultural program, twenty hands shot up with alacrity. Nobody hesitated; everyone was eager and quick. Alacrity is cheerful readiness, doing something promptly and willingly. Compare that to how slowly the same students answer when asked to solve a math problem.

en: Having mixed or contradictory feelings about something
hook: AMBI = both (ambidextrous). Feeling BOTH ways at once.
story: Rafi got admission to a university in Canada. He was thrilled about the opportunity, but he was also sad about leaving his parents and friends. He felt ambivalent: happy and sad at once, pulled in two directions. Ambivalent means having mixed, conflicting feelings. It does not mean indifferent; an ambivalent person feels a lot, just in opposite directions.

en: To make a bad situation better
hook: AMELIORATE: 'meliorate' sounds like 'better' (meilleur in French). Make better.
story: The village had no clean drinking water, and children kept getting sick. An NGO installed tube wells and taught families to boil water. Within a year, the situation was ameliorated; disease rates dropped sharply. To ameliorate is to improve a bad or unpleasant condition. It's a favorite GRE word for policies that make problems less severe.

en: Open and willing to be persuaded or to cooperate
hook: AMENABLE: says 'AMEN' readily, agreeing to your suggestion.
story: Mitu expected a fight when she asked her father to let her study abroad. But he was surprisingly amenable. He listened, asked a few questions, and agreed to support her. An amenable person is open to suggestions and easy to persuade. If your boss is amenable to remote work, you're lucky.

en: Belonging to a different time period; out of date
hook: ANA = against, CHRONO = time. Against its time.
story: In a historical drama set in the Mughal era, a careful viewer spotted a wristwatch on the emperor's arm. The internet exploded with jokes about the anachronistic mistake. Anachronistic means placed in the wrong time period. Today, using a fax machine in an office feels anachronistic too, like something left over from the past.

en: Showing bold willingness to take risks; daringly bold (sometimes rude)
hook: AUDACIOUS: 'AUDACity' — the nerve to do something bold.
story: With two balls left and twelve runs needed, the young batsman did something audacious. He switched hands and reverse-swept the fast bowler for six. The crowd gasped. It was risky, daring, and brilliant. Audacious describes a bold, daring act. It can be admiring, as here, or critical, as when someone shows audacity by lying to your face.

en: Extremely greedy for money or wealth
hook: AVARICIOUS: 'I've got to have my RICHES!'
story: The landlord was avaricious. He raised the rent every six months, charged tenants for broken pipes he never fixed, and kept every security deposit. No amount of money was ever enough for him. Avaricious means intensely greedy for wealth. Avarice is a classic sin in stories, and the greedy character usually loses everything in the end.

en: So common and unoriginal that it is boring
hook: BANAL: as boring as a BANANA, which you've eaten a thousand times.
story: Arif's GRE essay began, 'Since the dawn of time, humans have always…' The tutor sighed. 'This opening is banal; every second student writes it.' Banal means so ordinary and overused that it has lost any interest. Banal small talk, banal song lyrics, banal advice like 'just be yourself': all predictable and boring.

en: Gentle and kind; not harmful
hook: BENE = good (benefit). BENIGN = good-natured, harmless.
story: The doctor smiled and said, 'Don't worry, the lump is benign. It won't spread and it isn't dangerous.' Sara's family finally breathed again. In medicine, benign means harmless, the opposite of malignant. For people, benign means kind and gentle, like a benign old teacher who never shouts at anyone.

en: Bold and shameless, without any embarrassment
hook: BRAZEN: hard and shiny like BRASS, shameless.
story: The student copied answers from his neighbor's sheet in full view of the invigilator, then smiled at her. It was a brazen act of cheating, done openly, without the slightest shame. Brazen means bold in a shameless way. A brazen lie is one told directly to your face, even though both of you know it's false.

en: A false statement made to damage someone's reputation; slander
hook: CALUMNY sounds like 'CALL YOU MONEY-thief', a lie that ruins your name.
story: Before the election, anonymous posts claimed that the candidate had stolen relief funds. Not a single word was true; it was pure calumny, spread to destroy her reputation. Calumny means a false and damaging accusation. Truth eventually came out, but the calumny had already cost her many votes.

en: Truthful and straightforward; frank
hook: CANDID camera: it catches you as you really are, no filter.
story: 'Be candid with me,' Tanvir said, handing his essay to his professor. 'Is it good enough for Harvard?' She was. 'Your ideas are strong, but your writing is messy. Fix it.' It hurt, but he appreciated the honesty. A candid person tells the truth openly. A candid photo captures people naturally, without posing.

en: To criticize or scold someone severely
hook: CASTIGATE: sounds like 'cast out at the gate', thrown out with harsh words.
story: After the team lost five matches in a row, the coach castigated the players in the dressing room. He shouted for twenty minutes about lazy fielding and careless batting. Nobody dared reply. To castigate is to criticize harshly, to tear someone apart with words. Newspapers often castigate governments for failures.

en: Able to burn or corrode chemically; sarcastically bitter and hurtful
hook: CAUSTIC soda burns your skin; caustic words burn your feelings.
story: In chemistry lab, the teacher warned that caustic soda could burn their skin. Later that day, the same students experienced a different kind of burn: a caustic review of their project. 'Did you even try?' the examiner wrote. Caustic describes chemicals that corrode and comments that sting with bitter sarcasm.

en: To interpret or understand the meaning of something in a particular way
hook: CONSTRUE is the verb of CONSTRUCTION: how you construct the meaning.
story: Nadia didn't reply to her friend's message for two days because she was busy. Her friend construed the silence as anger and stopped talking to her. One small delay, interpreted the wrong way, caused a week of tension. To construe is to interpret or understand something in a particular way. Silence is easily misconstrued.

en: Feeling deep regret and guilt for having done wrong
hook: CONTRITE: sounds like 'contrition' — a confession full of regret.
story: After breaking his mother's favorite glass bowl and hiding the pieces, Rafi couldn't sleep. In the morning, he confessed with tears in his eyes and offered to buy a new one with his savings. He was truly contrite. Contrite means sincerely sorry and remorseful, not just apologizing because you were caught.

en: Extremely complex and difficult to follow
hook: CONVOLUTED: like a coiled-up VOLUTE, twisted spiral.
story: The government's new tax form was so convoluted that even accountants were confused. Section B referred to section F, which referred back to section A, with exceptions on page twelve. Convoluted means complicated and twisted, hard to understand. GRE reading passages often have convoluted sentences, so break them into smaller parts.

en: To desire something that belongs to someone else
bn: লোভ করা; অন্যের জিনিস পেতে চাওয়া
hook: COVET: you want to put a COVER over their thing and take it home.
story: Every time Arif saw his classmate's new iPhone, he felt a sharp pang of desire. He stared at it during lectures and dreamed about it at night. He coveted that phone. To covet is to want strongly, especially something that belongs to someone else. In GRE terms, a coveted prize is one that many people desperately want.

en: Contemptibly cowardly
hook: CRAVEN: the opposite of a brave RAVEN, it flies away at any danger.
story: When the thief snatched an old woman's bag, a strong young man standing nearby simply turned and walked away, pretending he hadn't seen anything. Later, people called his behavior craven, shamefully cowardly. Craven is stronger than scared; it suggests disgusting cowardice. A craven leader avoids every difficult decision to save himself.

en: Behavior that is polite, proper, and appropriate to the situation
hook: DECORUM is related to DECORATE: decent, proper presentation.
story: At the funeral, everyone spoke softly and dressed in white. Then someone's phone blasted loud music, and the man laughed loudly while turning it off. Elders glared at him for breaking decorum. Decorum means proper, dignified behavior. Courtrooms, exam halls, and weddings all have their own rules of decorum.

en: Quick and skillful, especially with the hands
hook: DEFT sounds like the opposite of DAFT: not stupid, but skilled.
story: The street-food vendor was deft. With a few quick flicks of his wrist, he flipped parathas, cracked eggs, and wrapped orders in paper without ever looking down. Customers watched in awe. Deft means skillful and quick. A deft politician handles difficult questions smoothly; a deft surgeon moves with perfect precision.

en: To raise doubts or politely object
hook: DEMUR: 'Hmm, de-MURmur', a hesitant, quiet objection.
story: When the team leader proposed working all weekend, Sara demurred. 'I'm not sure that's necessary,' she said quietly. 'Could we finish by Thursday instead?' She didn't fight; she politely objected. To demur is to express mild reluctance or doubt. Don't confuse it with demure, which means modest and shy.

en: Copied or imitated from others; not original
hook: DERIVATIVE: DERIVED from someone else's work.
story: The new action movie had a hero who looked like Batman, a villain who talked like the Joker, and a plot borrowed from Mission Impossible. Critics called it derivative, nothing new, just pieces of older films glued together. Derivative means imitative and unoriginal. On the GRE, 'derivative' art is the opposite of innovative art.

en: To remove all the moisture from; to dry out completely
hook: DESICCATE: think DESERT — dry. Also desiccated coconut, the dried kind.
story: In the drought, the fields cracked open, the river shrank to mud, and the rice plants turned brown and brittle. The sun had desiccated the entire village. To desiccate is to dry something out completely. Desiccated coconut is coconut with all its moisture removed, which is why it lasts so long on the shelf.

en: A forceful, bitter verbal attack
hook: DIATRIBE: a speech that would make a whole TRIBE DIE of embarrassment.
story: After his phone was stolen on the bus, Uncle Jamal delivered a twenty-minute diatribe against the government, the police, the transport system, and young people in general. Nobody could interrupt. A diatribe is a long, angry, bitter attack in speech or writing. It's more than criticism; it's a furious outburst.

en: Unwilling or unable to believe something
bn: অবিশ্বাসী; বিশ্বাস করতে পারছে না এমন
hook: IN-CRED-ulous: NO CREDit given to the claim; he doesn't believe it.
story: When Mitu told her friends she had scored 330 on the GRE, they stared at her, incredulous. 'No way. Show us the score report!' They simply couldn't believe it. Incredulous means skeptical, unable to believe. Don't confuse it with incredible, which describes something hard to believe, not the person doubting it.

en: Innocent, trusting, and naive; childlike in simplicity
hook: IN-GENU-ous: genuine, innocent, without tricks. Not to be confused with ingenious (clever).
story: Arif's little sister was ingenuous. When a stranger online claimed to be a prince who needed her help, she believed every word and almost sent him her pocket money. She trusted people completely. Ingenuous means innocently naive. Remember: ingenious means clever; ingenuous means simple and trusting.
